title: Yekaterinoslav to London: The Wanderings of the Sphinx of the Nineteenth Century
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Yekaterinoslav, the Fadeyev house, on the night of the cholera
stops.campa: In the house of the Fadeyevs on the Dnieper, while the cholera walks the streets and empties the churches, a daughter is born to Helena Andreyevna and Captain Peter von Hahn. The mother, herself half-dead of the plague, cannot rise; the priest circling the font trails his robe into a candle and sets the vestments alight, and the infant in the water is passed through fire on her first day. The nurses read it at once as an omen: this child will pass her whole life through burnings and be scorched by none of them. She is baptised Helena Petrovna, and the century has met its Sphinx.
suggested_refs: The Fadeyev house, Dnipro (Blavatsky birthplace museum)
Portrait of H. P. Blavatsky as a young woman
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Saratov, the subterranean corridors and the invisible playmates
stops.campa: The wild girl builds a tower of broken chairs beneath a barred window in the cellar-corridors of the governor's house, and there she is never alone. A troupe of playmates no adult can see keeps her company; her favourite is a small hunchback who leads her into endless mischief. She walks and talks in her sleep, and swears that eyes glare at her out of the furniture and the walls. Above them all stands a majestic Hindu in a white turban whom she calls her Protector, watching over the barred window. The servants cross themselves; the family calls it nerves. She knows it is not.
suggested_refs: Illustrations to Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Tiflis, the betrothal to the vice-governor
stops.campa: At the house of her aunt Yekaterina de Witte in Tiflis, seventeen and untamed, Helena is betrothed to Nikifor Blavatsky, a state official three times her age soon to be vice-governor of Erevan. She has boasted she could no more marry the old man than an old crow, and to spite a governess who told her no man would have her, she now accepts him. But the vow she makes is inward and against him: he shall never be a husband to her. The trap of the marriage closes even as she signs herself into it, and she is already planning the flight.
suggested_refs: The de Witte family of the Caucasus
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Djelal-Oghlu, the marriage fled
stops.campa: Married on the seventh of July in the shadow of the Erevan mountains, she keeps her vow: the marriage is never consummated. Within weeks she is on horseback and gone, over the passes toward the coast, servants scandalised and family shamed behind her. She reaches the Black Sea, bribes her way onto an English sailing-bark bound for Constantinople, and slips out of the whole Russian world at eighteen. The runaway bride becomes, in a single flight, the wanderer she will be for the rest of her life. No governor, no husband, no border will hold her again.
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Constantinople, the first freedom
stops.campa: In Constantinople the escaped bride finds her feet. She falls in with Countess Kisselev and a circus-rider's world of adventurers, and by her own account rides bareback in the ring for money when the purse runs thin. From here she moves through Greece, Egypt and the Levant with the Countess, a girl of eighteen loose in the East with no chaperone and no plan but forward. The Ottoman capital is the hinge: behind it lies the Russia she fled, ahead the decades of wandering. She has become no one's, and therefore free to become anyone's pupil.
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: London, Hyde Park: the Master Morya in the flesh
stops.campa: On her twentieth birthday, among the crowds of the Great Exhibition, Helena sees walking in the flesh the tall Hindu of her childhood dreams: the Protector of the barred window, come to London with a delegation of Indian princes. She nearly rushes to him; he stops her with a glance, then bids her meet him in Hyde Park. There, seated beside her, Master Morya tells her of the work for which she was born: he needs her cooperation for a task before her, and she must spend three years in Tibet to prepare. She gives her word. The mission of her life is sealed on a park bench.
stops.quote: I saw Master in my visions ever since my childhood... He ordered me to meet Him in Hyde Park.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, letter to A. P. Sinnett (Sinnett, The Letters of H. P. Blavatsky to A. P. Sinnett)
suggested_refs: The Crystal Palace, Great Exhibition of 1851
sources: The Letters of H. P. Blavatsky to A. P. Sinnett

stops.name: New Orleans and the voodoo of the bayous
stops.campa: Under the Master's charge to wander before she is ready, she crosses to the Americas and comes down into New Orleans, drawn to the voodoo of the Black congregations and the sorcery of the swamps. She studies the rites at close hand, hungry for any door into the hidden powers, until, she will say, the Master warns her in a dream of the dark forces she is playing with, and she breaks off and flees the city. The lesson stays: the phenomena are real, but not all hands that raise them are clean. She turns her face toward the deeper South.
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: The Andes and the ruins of Peru
stops.campa: Through Mexico and Central America and down the Pacific coast she rides to Peru, into the dead cities of a vanished race. Among the Andean ruins she reads the signs of a civilisation older and wiser than the conquerors who broke it, and gathers proofs, she will insist, of the single archaic wisdom that once lit every continent before the Flood of history drowned it. The stones of the Incas speak to her of Atlantis and of ages lost. What she carries away is not gold but a thesis: that all the world's temples are shards of one broken lamp.
suggested_refs: Inca ruins of Cusco and the Sacred Valley
Isis Unveiled, chapters on the Americas
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

segments.name: The Veiled Years Beyond the Himalaya

stops.name: Darjeeling, the border barred
stops.campa: Sent back from the New World toward the East, she comes at last to the roof of the world and tries the door. At the Darjeeling frontier the British turn her back; the way into forbidden Tibet is shut to a lone European woman, and the guardians of the passes do not yet open. She is not ready, and the mountains know it. She withdraws, wanders on through India and beyond, biding the years until the summons comes and the road that no map shows will finally lie open before her feet. The three years the Master named have not yet begun.
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Kashmir, into Tibet with the Tartar shaman
stops.campa: This time the door opens. Guided by a Tartar shaman who is hurrying home to his own country, disguised and travelling rough through Kashmir and Ladakh, she crosses at last into Little Tibet. On the road the shaman lays her flat with a fever and, by a rite over a lake and a mirror of polished metal, calls up the living image of his own village a thousand miles away for her to see. She has entered the closed land at the feet of the hidden Brotherhood, and the country of the Masters receives her as one long expected.
suggested_refs: Isis Unveiled, vol. II: the Tartar shaman's mirror
sources: H. P. Blavatsky, Isis Unveiled, vol. II

stops.name: Mentana, five wounds for Garibaldi
stops.campa: Between the Tibetan sojourns she turns up on a battlefield. At Mentana, where Garibaldi's redshirts break against the papal and French rifles, she stands among the volunteers and is cut down: a ball in the shoulder, a shattered arm, a broken leg, and left for dead among the corpses until she is dragged out alive. She keeps the scars and shows them for the rest of her life as proof she was there. The woman of the astral planes bleeds red on the road to Rome; the seer is also a soldier, and both wounds are true in this telling.
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Shigatse, the ashram of the Masters near Tashilhunpo
stops.campa: Beyond the Himalaya, in the valley of Shigatse under the golden roofs of Tashilhunpo, she comes to rest at last in the house of Master Koot Hoomi, near the seat of the Panchen Lama. Here dwell the Mahatmas: Morya and Koot Hoomi, Kashmiris of the Punjab, adepts of the Gelugpa way who have kept the archaic wisdom alive while the outer world forgot it. She lives at their feet, learns the discipline of the astral senses, and studies the Book of Dzyan, the oldest book on earth, whose verses she will one day give to the West. This is the hidden heart of the whole journey.
suggested_refs: Portraits of the Mahatmas Morya and Koot Hoomi
sources: The Letters of H. P. Blavatsky to A. P. Sinnett

stops.name: Shigatse, the Master's letter to the family at Odessa
stops.campa: In Odessa the aunt Nadyezhda, sick with two years' silence and fearing Helena dead, opens a letter that no post carried and no hand delivered. It simply appears. Written in French in a fine unknown script and signed with a Rajput name, it bids the family be at peace: their beloved is safe, far away in a retreat beyond reach, and shall be restored to them. Master Koot Hoomi has spoken across half the earth to comfort her people. The letter becomes a family relic and the first of the phenomena the world will later fight over. The Brotherhood, it says plainly, is real.
stops.quote: The noble relations of Mad. H. Blavatsky have no cause whatever for grief. Their daughter and niece has not left this world at all.
stops.quote_source: The Koot Hoomi letter to Nadyezhda Fadeyev, 1870 (Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky)
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Off Spetsai, the wreck of the Eumonia
stops.campa: Sailing from Piraeus toward Egypt aboard the steamer Eumonia, she is caught in disaster when the ship's powder or fireworks cargo blows apart off the island of Spetsai. The vessel is torn open and most aboard are drowned or burned; she is flung into the sea and comes ashore with nothing: no money, no luggage, only her life. Passed again through fire and water and unscathed, as the font foretold, she reaches Alexandria a penniless survivor. The sea has stripped her to begin again, and she goes up to Cairo to raise the dead of a different kind.
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Cairo, the Société Spirite founders in scandal
stops.campa: In Cairo she founds a Société Spirite to test the mediums and sift the true from the false in the fashionable spirit-craze. It collapses inside a fortnight: the hired mediums drink, cheat, and produce their marvels with gauze and wire; a madman breaks in upon a séance; the money vanishes. Here too she first meets Emma Cutting, the future Madame Coulomb, who lends her cash and will one day become her destroyer. She writes home in disgust that the spooks of the séance-room are no spirits at all but the cast-off skins of the dead. She has learned the fraud from the inside.
stops.quote: Their spirits are no spirits but spooks — rags, the cast off second skins of their personalities that the dead shed in the astral light as serpents shed theirs on earth.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, letter of 1872 (from Cairo)

stops.name: New York, landing penniless at the Master's order
stops.campa: The order comes from the Master while she is in Paris: go to America. On the seventh of July she steps off the ship at New York with almost nothing in her purse, and when she sees a poor woman in worse straits she gives away her last coin. For a season the future oracle of the age lives in a tenement and sews cravats and makes artificial flowers for her bread. She waits, as she has learned to wait, knowing the summons will make sense in its own time. The New World that will make her famous first makes her a seamstress.
suggested_refs: Castle Garden immigrant landing, New York
sources: A. P. Sinnett, Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky

stops.name: Chittenden, Vermont: the meeting with Olcott at the Eddy farm
stops.campa: At the Eddy brothers' haunted farmstead in Vermont, where spirit-forms are said to walk nightly out of a cabinet, she comes to see the phenomena, and to be seen. Henry Steel Olcott, a Civil-War colonel turned investigating journalist, notices the Russian in the red Garibaldi shirt across the room, offers her a light for her cigarette, and the great collaboration of both their lives ignites over a match. Within days the phenomena at the farm grow strange and vivid in her presence. The soldier of Rome has found her second soldier; together they will found a Society and remake the spiritual map of the West.
suggested_refs: Henry Steel Olcott, People from the Other World (1875)
sources: H. S. Olcott, Old Diary Leaves, vol. I

stops.name: New York, the founding of the Theosophical Society
stops.campa: In her rooms at Irving Place, after George Felt's lecture on the lost canon of proportion in the Egyptian temples, the talk turns to founding a body to study the hidden side of nature and the powers latent in man. Olcott passes a note proposing a society; Judge seconds it; Helena assents. Within days the name is chosen, Theosophical, meaning the divine wisdom, and on the seventeenth of November it is launched to the public with Olcott as President and Blavatsky its living oracle. From a New York parlour a movement is born that will carry the word of the Masters around the earth.
suggested_refs: The founding minutes of the Theosophical Society, 1875
sources: H. S. Olcott, Old Diary Leaves, vol. I

stops.name: The Lamasery: Isis Unveiled written under dictation
stops.campa: In the cluttered flat on Forty-Seventh Street they call the Lamasery, hung with Eastern silks, a stuffed baboon in a wing-collar clutching lecture notes in mockery of Darwin, where she writes Isis Unveiled through the nights. She quotes books she has never opened and cannot have; passages appear before her in the air and she copies them down; the Master, she says, dictates and her hand obeys. Twelve hundred pages come forth, and a thousand copies sell in ten days. Her first great work declares one primeval wisdom-religion beneath all faiths, and the veil of the goddess is lifted for the modern world.
stops.quote: The work now submitted to public judgment is the fruit of a somewhat intimate acquaintance with Eastern adepts and study of their science.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, Isis Unveiled (1877), preface

stops.name: Bombay, the Founders arrive in the land of the Masters
stops.campa: The Master's order to leave for India comes, and the two Founders sail. On the sixteenth of February Blavatsky and Olcott step ashore at Bombay and kiss the ground of the sacred land, the first Western spiritual teachers to come to India not to convert her but to sit at her feet. They take a house on Girgaum Back Road, hire the boy Babula, and open the true headquarters of the movement in the country of its origin. Hindus and Parsis flock to the strange Russian who honours their scriptures above the missionaries' Bible. The tide of Theosophy turns eastward, homeward, at last.
suggested_refs: H. S. Olcott, Old Diary Leaves: the Indian arrival
sources: H. S. Olcott, Old Diary Leaves, vol. II

stops.name: Allahabad and the meeting of Sinnett and Hume
stops.campa: At Allahabad she wins the two Englishmen who will make the Masters famous and infamous. A. P. Sinnett, editor of the Pioneer, and A. O. Hume of the Indian Civil Service open their houses and their minds to her, hungry for proof of the Brotherhood. Through her they begin to correspond with Morya and Koot Hoomi themselves, letters passing by no earthly post. Out of this contact will come Sinnett's Occult World and Esoteric Buddhism, and the whole archive of Mahatma letters. She has handed the hidden Masters two English pens; the phenomena are about to go to press.
sources: A. P. Sinnett, The Occult World

stops.name: Kandy, Ceylon: taking the Buddhist pansil
stops.campa: In Ceylon, before the monks and a great crowd, Blavatsky and Olcott kneel and take pansil, the five precepts, and become, formally and publicly, Buddhists, the first Westerners of note to do so on Buddhist soil. The island rejoices; the Sinhalese see in these two white foreigners defenders sent to raise their faith against the missionaries. Olcott will go on to design the Buddhist flag and write the catechism; Blavatsky lends the movement her fame. The wanderer who studied at Tashilhunpo now bows to the Dharma in the open, and the East claims her as its own.
sources: H. S. Olcott, Old Diary Leaves, vol. II

stops.name: Simla, the phenomena of the brooch and the cup
stops.campa: In the hill-station of Simla she makes the wonders that will ring round the Empire. At a picnic where a seventh guest lacks a cup, she holds a silent word with a Brother, points into the ground, and a china cup and saucer are dug from the untouched earth. A brooch that Mrs. Sinnett left at home is found sewn inside a cushion no one has opened. A note torn and vanished from her hand reappears among the branches of a tree, signed in Tibetan characters. Sinnett prints it all in The Occult World, and the astonished West sends its investigators east to catch her out.
suggested_refs: The Occult World: the cup-and-saucer, the brooch
sources: A. P. Sinnett, The Occult World

stops.name: Sikkim, the Master seen in the mountains
stops.campa: Dying of a kidney disease that has nearly stopped her heart, she is called north to the border of Sikkim and there, on the edge of the forbidden land, she meets Master Morya in his own body, not a vision but the man, warm and living, who heals her with a look and gives her the strength to go on. She comes back down transfigured, the illness lifted, witnesses swearing she left a wreck and returned whole. The Brotherhood is not a memory of Tibet but a present power that reaches down out of the snows to keep its instrument alive for the work still unwritten.
sources: The Letters of H. P. Blavatsky to A. P. Sinnett

stops.name: Adyar, the headquarters and the Shrine
stops.campa: On the banks of the Adyar river near Madras the Society buys its permanent home, a great house among palms and banyans, and the headquarters moves down from Bombay. In an upper room hangs the Shrine: a cabinet where letters placed inside are answered by the Masters and precipitated replies appear in Koot Hoomi's hand. Chelas come and go; the phenomena multiply; the Occult Room becomes the sacred centre of the movement's world. Here Blavatsky reigns as the living mouthpiece of the Brotherhood, and here, in the same room, the trap that will nearly end her is even now being built into the wall.
stops.quote: There is no religion higher than truth.
stops.quote_source: Motto of the Theosophical Society (Satyât Nâsti Paro Dharmah), adopted 1880; on the title-page of The Secret Doctrine
suggested_refs: The Shrine of the Occult Room
sources: H. S. Olcott, Old Diary Leaves

segments.name: The Coulomb Trial and the Verdict of the Age

stops.name: Paris, the Master's hand across Europe
stops.campa: Called to Europe to answer the growing storm, she settles for a season in Paris, feted by duchesses and hunted by journalists, while Judge crosses the ocean to help her and the Masters' letters keep falling from the air into astonished drawing-rooms. She lectures, she astonishes, she gathers the London Lodge to her. But behind her at Adyar the servants she trusted are turning: Emma Coulomb, the woman who fed her in Cairo, is selling to the missionaries a bundle of letters that will be read as the confession of a lifetime's fraud. The triumph in Paris is the calm before the knife.
sources: H. S. Olcott, Old Diary Leaves

stops.name: Adyar, the trapdoors behind the Shrine
stops.campa: In the Founders' absence the Coulombs are cast out of Adyar, and Alexis Coulomb leaves behind, or has built, a sliding panel, a secret passage, and trapdoors in the wall behind the Shrine, by which, the missionaries now say, the Masters' letters were slipped in by human hands all along. The Christian College Magazine of Madras prints Emma's letters as proof that the phenomena were conjuring and Blavatsky the conjuror. The sacred cabinet is torn out and burned by frightened officials. The holy centre of the movement becomes Exhibit One, and the whole edifice of the Masters is put on trial before the world.

stops.name: Adyar, Hodgson comes to judge
stops.campa: The London Society for Psychical Research sends out Richard Hodgson, a young Cambridge man, to sift the wonders at their source. He measures the walls, weighs the letters, listens to the missionaries and the Coulombs, and studies the Mahatma hand against Blavatsky's own. He leaves persuaded that Morya and Koot Hoomi never wrote a line: that the woman herself, gifted beyond any common forger, penned every letter and staged every marvel. In this register the tragedy is double: the Masters are true, and the earnest young investigator, deceived by their enemies, condemns the truest witness of the age as its cleverest liar.

stops.name: London, the SPR verdict: 'one of the most accomplished impostors'
stops.campa: In December the Society for Psychical Research prints Hodgson's two hundred pages, and the sentence of the age is passed: neither a nobody nor a mere tool of others, Madame Blavatsky is set down for history as one of the most accomplished, ingenious, and interesting impostors that ever lived. The learned world closes the case; the newspapers gloat; the movement reels. She had resigned her office and been carried half-dead to Europe rather than face a trial that would drag the Masters into court. The verdict will stand a hundred years, until, in 1986, the same Society confesses she was unjustly condemned.
stops.quote: one of the most accomplished, ingenious, and interesting impostors in history.
stops.quote_source: Richard Hodgson, Report of the Committee appointed to investigate Phenomena connected with the Theosophical Society (SPR, 1885)
suggested_refs: Vernon Harrison, H.P.B. and the SPR (1997)

segments.name: The Secret Doctrine and the Last Disciples

stops.name: Würzburg, the Secret Doctrine begun
stops.campa: Broken in health and name, exiled from her India, she takes rooms in Würzburg, and the Countess Wachtmeister comes to keep her. And here, out of the ashes of the scandal, the greatest work begins. Night after night she writes The Secret Doctrine, drawing on the Book of Dzyan and, she says, on the astral scrolls the Masters open before her eyes; the Countess watches passages appear on blank paper and material she could not own materialise on the desk. From the ruin the largest structure rises. The impostor of the newspapers is building the scripture of a new age with a dead woman's discipline.
sources: C. Wachtmeister, Reminiscences of H. P. Blavatsky and The Secret Doctrine

stops.name: Ostend, the coma and the choice to live
stops.campa: At Ostend, on the flat Belgian coast, the kidney disease closes over her at last and she falls into a coma the doctors call death's door. In the dark she is given the choice: to let go and be free of the tortured body, or to return and finish the book that the world needs. She chooses to come back. She wakes to the astonished physician and takes up her pen again, a woman who has, in her own telling, refused death itself for the sake of the Secret Doctrine. The Keightley brothers come to carry her and her three-foot stack of manuscript across to London.
sources: C. Wachtmeister, Reminiscences of H. P. Blavatsky and The Secret Doctrine

stops.name: London, Lansdowne Road: The Secret Doctrine published
stops.campa: From Lansdowne Road in Holland Park, with the Keightleys ordering her mountain of pages into volumes, The Secret Doctrine comes off the press: the synthesis of science, religion and philosophy, the seven Stanzas of Dzyan unveiled at last, the story of the root-races and the ages of the world. Five hundred copies are sold before the day of publication. Beginning in the deep, before worlds, the eternal parent wrapped in her ever-invisible robes, slumbering through seven eternities, she gives the West its cosmogony. The impostor's masterwork becomes the great grimoire of the coming century.
stops.quote: The Eternal Parent wrapped in her ever-invisible robes had slumbered once again for seven Eternities.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine (1888), Stanza I of Dzyan
sources: H. P. Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine

stops.name: London, the Esoteric Section and the inner school
stops.campa: Around her at Lansdowne Road, and then at Avenue Road, she gathers the Blavatsky Lodge and founds the Esoteric Section: the inner school for those who would not merely study but be trained, pledged to her and through her to the Masters. She issues the magazine Lucifer, the Light-Bringer, to bring hidden things to light, and answers her disciples' questions night after night in sessions they write down as scripture. The old warrior, dropsical and half-crippled, holds a court of seekers. Here, in these last rooms, the transmission she carried out of Tibet is handed on to the ones who will keep the link.
suggested_refs: The Transactions of the Blavatsky Lodge
sources: H. P. Blavatsky, The Key to Theosophy

stops.name: London, Annie Besant crosses over
stops.campa: The great freethinker and firebrand Annie Besant, secularist and champion of the poor, is given The Secret Doctrine to review and is undone by it. She comes to Avenue Road to meet the author, looks into the deep grey eyes, and surrenders a life of unbelief in an afternoon. On the tenth of May she signs the roll of the Society; soon she takes the pledge of the Esoteric Section and becomes the chosen heir. The scandal-broken exile has won the most formidable woman in England to the Masters' cause. In Besant the link will pass unbroken into the next century, out to India and Adyar again.
stops.quote: All who keep an open door to Truth will give scrutiny to any visitant, be the garb of Asia or of Europe, be the tongue of Paris or of Ind.
stops.quote_source: Annie Besant, review of The Secret Doctrine, Pall Mall Gazette, 25 April 1889
suggested_refs: Besant, Why I Became a Theosophist

stops.name: Fontainebleau: the Voice of the Silence
stops.campa: Resting in the forest of Fontainebleau, she pours out in two days, from memory of the Book of the Golden Precepts learned in the East, the small burning book she calls The Voice of the Silence: the heart-doctrine, the path of compassion for those who would renounce even Nirvana to stay and save the world. It is her gift to the mystics rather than the scholars, and of all her works the one the monks of the East most readily own as true. The warrior of phenomena ends as teacher of the silent road: thou canst not travel on the Path before thou hast become that Path itself.
stops.quote: Thou canst not travel on the Path before thou hast become that Path itself.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, The Voice of the Silence (1889), Fragment I
suggested_refs: The Voice of the Silence, first edition, 1889
sources: H. P. Blavatsky, The Voice of the Silence

stops.name: London, Avenue Road: 'Keep the link unbroken'
stops.campa: The influenza that is scything through London takes her at last at 19 Avenue Road, in her chair, on the eighth of May. Two nights before, waking suddenly, she had charged the disciple at her side with the whole burden of the future: keep the link unbroken, do not let my last incarnation be a failure. Now she is gone, and the day her people will keep forever as White Lotus Day. Her body is burned at Woking; her ashes are divided between New York, London, and Adyar, three cities of her wandering. The Sphinx of the century is silent; the Masters, she promised, are not.
stops.quote: Keep the link unbroken! Do not let my last incarnation be a failure.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, last message to the Esoteric School, recorded by those present, 6 May 1891

stops.name: Oxford, Max Müller and the East that answers back
stops.campa: From his chair at Oxford, the great Sanskritist Max Müller, master of the fifty volumes of the Sacred Books of the East, turns his authority against her. There is no esoteric Buddhism, he declares, no hidden doctrine behind the Shastras that could bear her Theosophy; her secret wisdom is folly and, worse, fraud, no sweet odour in the nostrils of true scholars. The academic East she claimed as her authority rises up to disown her. Yet the books she wrote outsell his; the Masters she carried out of Shigatse have already gone where his footnotes cannot follow, into the living faith of the coming age.
stops.quote: Esoteric Buddhism has no sweet odour in the nostrils of Sanskrit and Pali scholars.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Books of the East (50 vols.)

stops.name: Berlin, Steiner turns the stream to the West
stops.campa: Eleven years after her death, a young Austrian scholar, Rudolf Steiner, is made head of the German Section of her Society and reads her root-races and her hidden Masters with new eyes. He grows the German branch to thousands, but he wants a Western, Christian esoteric path, and he will not bow to the Eastern turn or the crowning of a boy as the World Teacher. In 1912 he breaks away to found Anthroposophy, carrying half her German disciples with him. The stream she poured out of Tibet splits at Steiner into an Eastern and a Western river, and both run on into the new century.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Anthroposophical Society, 1912-13

stops.name: Adyar, the ashes return; the link held
stops.campa: On the banks of the Adyar river a portion of her ashes comes home, and each May the Society she founded keeps White Lotus Day, reading from the Gita and the Voice of the Silence over the water. Annie Besant, president now, holds the movement she was given; Olcott is long buried in the same soil; the headquarters she chose still stands among the banyans. The link she charged them to keep is not broken. From a burning font at Yekaterinoslav to a river in Madras, the wanderer's ashes complete the last leg of the journey, and the Masters' seat in the world holds its ground.

stops.name: The esoteric descent, Savitri Devi and Miguel Serrano
stops.campa: Far down her lineage, where the light she carried is bent into a darkness she never meant, her root-races and her lost Aryan ages are taken up by others. In India, Savitri Devi weds Hindu cosmology to the myth of the master race and hails a fallen dictator as an avatar of the cycles; in Chile, the diplomat Miguel Serrano builds an esoteric Hitlerism of Thulean gods and cosmic war. They are the shadow-heirs of the Secret Doctrine, reading its cyclical ages into a creed of hatred. The atlas records the descent as it records the ascent: the same seed, in poisoned ground, bearing bitter fruit.
